questions.stem: A secreted factor acts on the same cell that released it. What is the mode?
questions.why: Autocrine signalling occurs when a cell releases a mediator that binds receptors on that same cell, modifying its own activity. This provides local self-regulation without requiring transport through the systemic circulation.

notes.B: Paracrine mediators act on nearby cells, rather than returning specifically to receptors on the cell that secreted them.
notes.C: Endocrine hormones travel through the bloodstream to reach distant target cells, unlike the local self-directed pathway described.
notes.D: Neurocrine signalling involves release of neuronal chemical messengers onto target cells, rather than necessarily acting on the secreting cell.
notes.E: Exocrine secretion delivers substances through ducts or onto epithelial surfaces, rather than regulating the secreting cell through receptor signalling.

questions.stem: A mediator diffuses to a neighbouring cell through interstitial fluid. What type of signalling is involved?
questions.why: Paracrine signalling involves local release of a mediator into extracellular fluid and diffusion to neighbouring target cells. Its action is limited by distance, degradation and uptake rather than depending on systemic circulation.

notes.A: Autocrine signalling describes a mediator acting back on its own secreting cell rather than primarily affecting a neighbouring cell.
notes.C: Endocrine signalling uses circulating blood to deliver hormones to distant target cells, rather than relying solely on local interstitial diffusion.
notes.D: Neurocrine signalling involves neuronal release of chemical messengers; the stem does not specify a neuronal source or synaptic pathway.
notes.E: Exocrine products are delivered to epithelial surfaces or through ducts, rather than acting as interstitial regulatory messengers between adjacent cells.

questions.stem: Which hormone is transported in plasma mainly without a protein carrier?
questions.why: Adrenaline is a relatively water-soluble catecholamine that circulates predominantly without a specialised high-affinity plasma carrier. Steroid and thyroid hormones are more extensively protein-bound, which influences their distribution, clearance and circulating half-lives.

notes.A: Cortisol circulates largely bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin and albumin, with a smaller free fraction available for receptor activation.
notes.B: Thyroxine is strongly bound to thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin and albumin, creating a substantial circulating reservoir of hormone.
notes.D: Aldosterone is less extensively protein-bound than cortisol but still circulates partly bound to albumin and other plasma proteins.
notes.E: Testosterone is substantially bound to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin because of its relatively lipophilic steroid structure.

questions.stem: An acute increase in thyroid-binding globulin first increases which hormone pool?
questions.why: An acute increase in thyroxine-binding globulin provides additional binding sites that temporarily draw free thyroxine into the protein-bound pool. Subsequent hypothalamic–pituitary feedback increases hormone production until free concentrations are restored.

notes.A: Additional binding sites initially tend to lower free plasma thyroxine, rather than directly raising its unbound concentration.
notes.B: Intracellular triiodothyronine depends on hormone delivery, transport and deiodination; increased circulating binding capacity does not directly increase this pool.
notes.C: Increased thyroxine-binding globulin can bind circulating triiodothyronine as well, but does not initially raise its unbound concentration.
notes.E: Protein binding retains hormone within the circulation and does not directly increase renal excretion of thyroxine.

questions.stem: Which hormone activates a cell-surface receptor with a second-messenger cascade?
questions.why: Glucagon is a peptide hormone whose receptor spans the target-cell membrane. In hepatocytes, receptor activation stimulates Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP-dependent protein kinase signalling, promoting mobilisation of stored metabolic fuel.

notes.A: Cortisol primarily binds an intracellular glucocorticoid receptor that regulates transcription, rather than requiring a conventional cell-surface second-messenger receptor.
notes.B: Thyroxine is converted partly to triiodothyronine, which principally acts through nuclear thyroid hormone receptors to regulate gene expression.
notes.C: Testosterone primarily signals through intracellular androgen receptors that modify transcription, although additional rapid non-genomic actions can occur.
notes.D: Calcitriol principally activates the intracellular vitamin D receptor, which regulates transcription of genes involved in mineral homeostasis.

questions.stem: Defective intracellular glucocorticoid receptors primarily impair which process?
questions.why: Cortisol diffuses into target cells and binds intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, which regulate gene expression through DNA interactions and other transcriptional mechanisms. Receptor dysfunction therefore primarily impairs cortisol-dependent genomic responses despite hormone availability.

notes.B: Rapid membrane depolarisation is generally mediated by changes in ion conductance, rather than the principal genomic action of glucocorticoid receptors.
notes.C: Calcium influx can trigger rapid secretory responses, but it is not the primary process mediated by intracellular cortisol receptors.
notes.D: Peptide exocytosis depends on vesicular machinery and intracellular calcium, rather than directly requiring the transcriptional function of glucocorticoid receptors.
notes.E: Plasma ligand clearance depends on metabolism, binding and excretion; receptor defects principally alter target-cell responsiveness rather than directly determining clearance.

questions.stem: A fall in plasma calcium directly raises PTH without pituitary stimulation. Which control is this?
questions.why: Parathyroid chief cells sense extracellular ionised calcium through the calcium-sensing receptor. A fall in calcium reduces receptor activation and increases parathyroid hormone secretion, demonstrating humoral control by a circulating mineral concentration.

notes.A: Neural regulation requires neuronal input to influence hormone release, whereas the calcium signal is detected directly by parathyroid cells.
notes.C: Tropic regulation involves stimulation by another hormone, such as pituitary TSH acting on the thyroid; this response requires no pituitary signal.
notes.D: Circadian regulation refers to secretion patterns linked to biological time, rather than an immediate response to reduced plasma calcium.
notes.E: Feedforward control anticipates a disturbance, whereas parathyroid hormone secretion responds to an existing calcium change through homeostatic feedback.

questions.stem: Why is a random GH sample often a poor measure of total secretion?
questions.why: Growth hormone secretion occurs in discrete pulses controlled by hypothalamic growth hormone-releasing hormone and somatostatin, with additional influences from sleep and metabolism. A single concentration may therefore capture a peak or trough rather than overall secretion.

notes.A: Constant secretion would make a random sample more representative, but growth hormone concentrations vary substantially throughout the day.
notes.B: Growth hormone-binding proteins influence circulating hormone distribution, but permanently fixed binding does not explain the major temporal variation in concentrations.
notes.D: Growth hormone is cleared through metabolic pathways, but the main sampling limitation is pulsatile secretion rather than episodic urinary excretion.
notes.E: Receptor saturation concerns target-cell responsiveness and cannot explain why plasma growth hormone concentrations fluctuate between secretory pulses.

questions.stem: Damage to hypothalamic portal vessels most directly reduces regulation of which secretion?
questions.why: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibitory hormones reach the anterior pituitary through its hypophyseal portal circulation. Disruption impairs thyrotropin-releasing hormone delivery and therefore normal regulation of anterior pituitary thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion.

notes.A: Vasopressin is synthesised in hypothalamic neurons and transported along axons to the posterior pituitary, rather than delivered through portal blood.
notes.B: Oxytocin travels along hypothalamic neurosecretory axons to posterior pituitary terminals, so its delivery does not depend directly on portal vessels.
notes.C: Adrenal medullary secretion is controlled principally by sympathetic preganglionic input, not hypothalamic releasing hormones transported through pituitary portal vessels.
notes.E: Parathyroid chief cells directly sense extracellular calcium and regulate PTH independently of anterior pituitary portal circulation.

questions.stem: Which structure synthesizes vasopressin before its storage in the posterior pituitary?
questions.why: Vasopressin is synthesised in magnocellular neurons of the hypothalamic supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. It is transported with neurophysin along axons to posterior pituitary terminals, where it is stored and released into blood.

notes.A: The posterior pituitary contains neurosecretory axon terminals that store and release vasopressin, rather than being its principal site of synthesis.
notes.B: Anterior pituitary endocrine cells synthesise hormones such as growth hormone and TSH, but vasopressin originates predominantly in hypothalamic neurons.
notes.C: Adrenal chromaffin cells produce catecholamines in response to sympathetic stimulation, rather than synthesising the posterior pituitary antidiuretic hormone.
notes.D: Pineal secretory cells synthesise melatonin, which participates in circadian regulation, rather than producing hypothalamic vasopressin for posterior pituitary storage.

questions.stem: Damage to the pituitary stalk prevents normal delivery of dopamine. Which hormone tends to rise?
questions.why: Hypothalamic dopamine reaches anterior pituitary lactotrophs through portal blood and tonically inhibits prolactin secretion via D2 receptors. Stalk disruption reduces this inhibitory input, commonly causing an increase in circulating prolactin.

notes.B: Thyrotropin secretion depends on hypothalamic TRH stimulation, which is disrupted by stalk damage rather than selectively released from dopamine inhibition.
notes.C: Somatotropin secretion depends on hypothalamic releasing and inhibitory signals; loss of stalk input does not typically produce the characteristic prolactin rise.
notes.D: Luteinising hormone requires pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH delivery, so interruption of this pathway commonly impairs rather than increases secretion.
notes.E: Follicle-stimulating hormone is regulated partly by GnRH and gonadal feedback; stalk damage usually disrupts its normal hypothalamic stimulation.

questions.stem: Which signal stimulates ADH release during simple water deprivation?
questions.why: Water deprivation increases effective plasma osmolality as water is lost relative to solute. Hypothalamic osmoreceptor activation promotes vasopressin release, increasing collecting-duct water permeability and reducing further urinary water loss.

notes.A: Reduced effective plasma osmolality suppresses osmotic stimulation of vasopressin, favouring excretion of excess water rather than conservation.
notes.C: Increased atrial filling signals greater central circulating volume and generally suppresses non-osmotic vasopressin release rather than stimulating it.
notes.D: Reduced plasma sodium usually lowers effective osmolality and therefore opposes osmotic vasopressin release unless other strong non-osmotic stimuli intervene.
notes.E: Glomerular filtration rate influences tubular fluid delivery, but it is not the primary hypothalamic signal during uncomplicated water deprivation.

questions.stem: Severe blood loss increases ADH without an initial change in osmolarity. What signal is responsible?
questions.why: Severe haemorrhage reduces arterial pressure and central vascular filling, decreasing stretch-sensitive baroreceptor afferent activity. This non-osmotic signal promotes vasopressin release even before plasma osmolality changes, helping conserve water and support circulation.

notes.A: Increased carotid sinus stretch indicates greater arterial pressure and generally suppresses compensatory vasopressin release rather than signalling haemorrhage.
notes.B: Increased atrial distension signals greater central blood volume, whereas haemorrhage reduces filling and activates volume-conserving mechanisms.
notes.D: Renal blood flow commonly decreases with substantial blood loss; increased flow is not the primary sensory signal initiating non-osmotic ADH release.
notes.E: Haemorrhage generally activates sympathetic catecholamine responses rather than reducing them; decreased baroreceptor firing is the relevant direct reflex signal.

questions.stem: A patient with persistent ADH excess retains water. Which result is expected?
questions.why: Persistent vasopressin action increases collecting-duct water reabsorption. When water intake continues and retained water exceeds solute retention, plasma sodium becomes diluted and effective plasma osmolality falls, producing hypotonic hyponatraemia.

notes.A: Hypernatraemia and hyperosmolality usually reflect water deficit relative to sodium, rather than disproportionate water retention under excessive vasopressin action.
notes.B: Sodium itself contributes substantially to effective plasma osmolality; disproportionate water retention typically reduces rather than raises plasma sodium concentration.
notes.C: Hypokalaemia and alkalosis are more characteristic of some mineralocorticoid-related disorders, rather than the primary dilutional consequence of vasopressin excess.
notes.E: Calcium and phosphate regulation depends chiefly on mineral-regulating hormones and renal handling, not the primary water-retaining effect of ADH.

questions.stem: Polyuria remains severe after desmopressin is given. Which defect best explains the observation?
questions.why: Desmopressin mimics vasopressin action at renal V2 receptors. Persistent polyuria despite adequate administration suggests nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, in which collecting ducts cannot respond appropriately to the hormone by increasing water permeability.

notes.A: Deficient hypothalamic vasopressin synthesis causes central diabetes insipidus, which generally responds to replacement with desmopressin when renal responsiveness is intact.
notes.B: Failure of posterior pituitary vasopressin release is another central cause and should usually improve when the missing hormone action is replaced.
notes.C: The kidney is a major vasopressin target rather than the normal source of circulating ADH; excess secretion would tend to conserve water.
notes.D: Increased pituitary hormone storage does not explain failure to respond to administered desmopressin, which bypasses the need for endogenous hormone release.

questions.stem: During suckling, which cells contract to expel milk already formed in alveoli?
questions.why: Suckling activates hypothalamic pathways that release oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin contracts mammary myoepithelial cells surrounding alveoli and small ducts, propelling previously synthesised milk towards the nipple.

notes.B: Alveolar secretory epithelial cells synthesise milk under prolactin and other hormonal influences, rather than primarily contracting to expel it.
notes.C: Stromal fibroblasts provide extracellular matrix and structural support, but are not the specialised contractile cells responsible for milk ejection.
notes.D: Anterior pituitary lactotrophs secrete prolactin, which promotes milk synthesis; they do not mechanically compress mammary alveoli during suckling.
notes.E: Ovarian granulosa cells participate in follicular development and steroid synthesis, rather than forming the contractile apparatus of mammary glands.

questions.stem: Cervical stretch causes oxytocin release, stronger contractions and more stretch. What loop is this?
questions.why: Cervical stretch activates sensory pathways promoting oxytocin release, which strengthens uterine contractions and causes further cervical stretch. This reinforcing cycle is positive feedback and terminates when delivery removes the initiating stimulus.

notes.A: Negative feedback counteracts the initiating change, whereas the described oxytocin response amplifies cervical stretch and uterine contraction.
notes.C: Tonic inhibition describes continuous suppressive input, rather than an escalating response in which the original stimulus becomes stronger.
notes.D: Delayed inhibition would eventually oppose the initiating stimulus, while the described labour mechanism repeatedly reinforces it until delivery.
notes.E: Receptor blockade would reduce oxytocin-mediated uterine contraction rather than account for the reinforcing stretch–contraction cycle.

questions.stem: What mediator accounts for much GH-driven growth of epiphyseal cartilage?
questions.why: Growth hormone stimulates production of insulin-like growth factor 1 in the liver and local tissues, including growth plates. IGF-1 promotes chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation, contributing substantially to longitudinal skeletal growth before epiphyseal fusion.

notes.A: Thyroid-stimulating hormone promotes thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion, rather than being the principal mediator of growth hormone action at cartilage.
notes.B: Adrenocorticotrophic hormone stimulates adrenal glucocorticoid production; excessive glucocorticoids can actually impair growth rather than mediate GH-dependent cartilage expansion.
notes.D: Parathyroid hormone regulates calcium and phosphate balance and influences bone remodelling, rather than serving as the primary GH-induced growth mediator.
notes.E: Corticotropin-releasing hormone stimulates pituitary ACTH release and regulates the stress axis, rather than transmitting growth hormone effects to epiphyseal cartilage.

questions.stem: A child has normal GH but markedly reduced hepatic IGF-1. Which response is most impaired?
questions.why: Growth hormone-induced circulating and locally produced IGF-1 contribute to growth-plate chondrocyte activity and linear skeletal growth. Markedly reduced hepatic IGF-1 can impair endocrine growth signalling, although locally produced IGF-1 and direct GH actions also contribute.

notes.A: Growth hormone can directly promote adipose lipolysis, so impaired circulating IGF-1 does not selectively abolish its fat-mobilising effects.
notes.B: Growth hormone has direct anti-insulin metabolic effects on glucose utilisation, rather than requiring IGF-1 for every reduction in cellular uptake.
notes.C: Increased fatty acid release from adipocytes is largely a direct metabolic action of growth hormone and may persist despite reduced hepatic IGF-1.
notes.E: Growth hormone promotes glucose sparing through direct metabolic effects, whereas longitudinal skeletal growth depends substantially on IGF-1 signalling.

questions.stem: Which factor suppresses rather than stimulates normal GH release?
questions.why: Acute hyperglycaemia normally suppresses growth hormone secretion through hypothalamic and metabolic regulatory pathways. This physiological suppression underlies the oral glucose suppression test used to assess inappropriate GH secretion in suspected acromegaly.

notes.A: Hypoglycaemia stimulates counter-regulatory growth hormone secretion, helping oppose insulin action and support availability of circulating metabolic fuels.
notes.B: Deep non-REM sleep is associated with major physiological growth hormone secretory pulses rather than sustained suppression of its release.
notes.C: Exercise commonly stimulates growth hormone secretion during and around recovery, depending on intensity, duration and metabolic conditions.
notes.D: Certain amino acids, particularly arginine, can stimulate growth hormone release; acute hyperglycaemia is the characteristic suppressive stimulus among these choices.

questions.stem: Why does chronic GH excess enlarge hands and jaw but not height in adults?
questions.why: After epiphyseal growth plates fuse, long bones cannot lengthen through growth-plate cartilage proliferation. Excess growth hormone and IGF-1 can still promote appositional bone growth and soft-tissue enlargement, producing acromegalic changes without increased adult height.

notes.B: Articular cartilage and other cartilaginous structures remain present in adults; disappearance of all cartilage is not required to stop linear growth.
notes.C: IGF-1 is generally increased in active acromegaly and contributes to tissue enlargement rather than ceasing after epiphyseal plate fusion.
notes.D: Growth hormone receptors remain functional in adult tissues, allowing excessive GH signalling to produce continued metabolic and structural changes.
notes.E: Periosteal and appositional bone growth can continue in adults and contributes to acromegalic enlargement, rather than being blocked.

questions.stem: A prolactinoma can cause amenorrhoea through which mechanism?
questions.why: Excess prolactin inhibits reproductive hypothalamic signalling, reducing pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion. The resulting reduction in gonadotropin drive impairs follicular maturation and ovulation, leading to menstrual irregularity or amenorrhoea.

notes.A: Amplifying the preovulatory LH surge would favour ovulation, whereas hyperprolactinaemia commonly disrupts the gonadotropin pattern necessary for normal ovulation.
notes.C: Ovarian aromatase supports oestrogen synthesis, but increased activity is not the principal mechanism of prolactin-induced reproductive-axis suppression.
notes.D: Enhanced follicular recruitment would not explain the usual hypogonadotropic response caused by excessive prolactin-mediated suppression of hypothalamic GnRH.
notes.E: Luteal growth follows ovulation and depends on gonadotropin support; hyperprolactinaemia can impair ovulatory and luteal function rather than accelerate them.

questions.stem: Why does copious milk secretion begin after delivery despite high prolactin in pregnancy?
questions.why: Placental delivery causes a marked fall in circulating progesterone, removing its inhibition of abundant milk synthesis despite previously elevated prolactin. In the presence of appropriate mammary development and hormonal support, this permits secretory activation after birth.

notes.A: Placental oestrogen concentrations fall after delivery rather than increase; withdrawal of placental steroids supports the transition to copious milk production.
notes.B: Human chorionic gonadotropin declines after placental delivery and is not the principal trigger that releases mammary lactogenesis from inhibition.
notes.D: Increased hypothalamic dopamine inhibits prolactin secretion, so it would tend to oppose rather than promote prolactin-supported milk synthesis.
notes.E: Loss of prolactin receptors would impair mammary responsiveness to prolactin rather than explain activation of copious milk secretion.

questions.stem: In primary adrenal failure, excess ACTH and skin pigmentation share which precursor?
questions.why: Pro-opiomelanocortin is processed into ACTH and other melanocortin-related peptides. In primary adrenal insufficiency, loss of cortisol feedback increases ACTH production; excessive melanocortin receptor stimulation promotes melanin synthesis and characteristic hyperpigmentation.

notes.A: Preproinsulin is processed into insulin and C-peptide in pancreatic beta cells, rather than supplying ACTH or melanocortin-related peptides.
notes.B: Angiotensinogen is cleaved by renin during regulation of vascular tone and aldosterone secretion, not processed into ACTH or melanocortins.
notes.C: Thyroglobulin provides the tyrosine residues used to synthesise thyroid hormones, rather than serving as a precursor for pituitary ACTH.
notes.E: Preproglucagon is processed into glucagon and related peptides in different tissues, rather than producing pituitary adrenocorticotrophic hormone.

questions.stem: Which transporter brings iodide into thyroid follicular cells against its gradient?
questions.why: The basolateral sodium–iodide symporter uses the inward sodium electrochemical gradient to accumulate iodide within thyroid follicular cells. Sodium–potassium ATPase maintains that gradient, making iodide uptake a secondary active process required for thyroid hormone synthesis.

notes.A: Sodium–glucose symporters use sodium gradients to transport glucose, rather than providing the specialised basolateral iodide uptake pathway in thyroid follicles.
notes.B: Sodium–calcium exchange regulates calcium handling in many cells, but it does not concentrate iodide for thyroid hormone synthesis.
notes.C: Potassium–chloride cotransport mediates coupled electrolyte movement and cell-volume regulation, rather than the selective sodium-dependent accumulation of iodide.
notes.D: Passive channels permit downhill ion movement, whereas the thyroid concentrates iodide through sodium-coupled transport against its own electrochemical gradient.

questions.stem: Which reactions in the colloid depend on thyroid peroxidase?
questions.why: Thyroid peroxidase at the apical follicular interface uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidise iodide, iodinate tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin and couple iodotyrosines. These reactions produce the hormone residues subsequently released as T3 and T4.

notes.B: Endocytosis and lysosomal proteolysis recover thyroid hormones from stored thyroglobulin; these steps do not represent the direct catalytic function of thyroid peroxidase.
notes.C: Iodothyronine deiodinases activate or inactivate thyroid hormones, while binding proteins transport them; thyroid peroxidase catalyses earlier synthetic reactions.
notes.D: Filtration and clearance regulate circulating substances but are not the colloid reactions directly catalysed by thyroid peroxidase during hormone synthesis.
notes.E: Vesicular exocytosis supplies thyroglobulin to colloid, and iodotyrosine recycling recovers iodide; neither process is thyroid peroxidase's principal catalytic action.

questions.stem: Coupling two diiodotyrosine residues produces which thyroid hormone?
questions.why: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses coupling of two diiodotyrosine residues within thyroglobulin to form a thyroxine residue containing four iodine atoms. Proteolytic processing of thyroglobulin subsequently releases thyroxine into the circulation.

notes.A: Triiodothyronine contains three iodine atoms and forms through coupling of monoiodotyrosine with diiodotyrosine in the appropriate orientation.
notes.C: Reverse T3 is an inactive triiodothyronine isomer generated mainly by inner-ring deiodination of thyroxine rather than coupling two diiodotyrosines.
notes.D: Monoiodotyrosine is formed by adding one iodine atom to a thyroglobulin tyrosine residue, rather than coupling two diiodotyrosine residues.
notes.E: Free iodide is an inorganic substrate for organification, rather than the iodinated hormone product created by coupling two diiodotyrosines.

questions.stem: A thionamide inhibits thyroid peroxidase. Which process is reduced most directly?
questions.why: Thionamides inhibit thyroid peroxidase-dependent iodide organification and iodotyrosine coupling, thereby reducing formation of newly synthesised T3 and T4. Previously stored iodinated thyroglobulin can still supply hormone, delaying the full clinical effect.

notes.A: Peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion is mediated by deiodinases; propylthiouracil can additionally inhibit this pathway, but it is distinct from thyroid peroxidase inhibition.
notes.B: Hypothalamic TRH is controlled through endocrine feedback and other neural signals, rather than being directly inhibited by blocking thyroid peroxidase.
notes.D: Hepatic plasma binding-protein synthesis influences hormone transport, but is not the immediate enzymatic target of thyroid peroxidase inhibition.
notes.E: Renal iodide filtration contributes to iodide elimination, whereas inhibition of thyroid peroxidase principally reduces incorporation of iodide into hormone precursors.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes thyroid hormone storage from most endocrine storage?
questions.why: Thyroid follicles store large amounts of iodinated thyroglobulin extracellularly within colloid. Hormone residues remain covalently incorporated into this protein until endocytosis and proteolysis release T3 and T4, providing a substantial reserve.

notes.A: Most stored thyroid hormone residues are incorporated into extracellular thyroglobulin rather than maintained as free triiodothyronine in intracellular secretory vesicles.
notes.B: Circulating protein-bound thyroxine provides a plasma reservoir, but the distinctive glandular storage mechanism occurs within extracellular follicular colloid.
notes.C: Iodide is incorporated into tyrosine residues within thyroglobulin, rather than stored primarily as intracellular crystals of inorganic iodide.
notes.E: Plasma and lymphatic binding proteins carry hormone after secretion; they do not account for the characteristic large intrafollicular thyroid hormone reserve.

questions.stem: TSH promotes T3 and T4 release from stored colloid mainly by what mechanism?
questions.why: Thyroid-stimulating hormone stimulates follicular cells to internalise iodinated thyroglobulin from colloid. Lysosomal proteases cleave the protein, releasing T3 and T4 for transport across the basolateral membrane into the circulation.

notes.A: Iodide oxidation occurs at the apical follicular interface during hormone synthesis, not in plasma during release of previously stored hormone.
notes.B: Thyroglobulin is secreted apically into colloid for hormone synthesis and storage; hormone release requires recovery and proteolysis of the stored protein.
notes.C: Hepatic binding proteins influence thyroid hormone transport after its release, rather than liberating hormone residues from follicular thyroglobulin.
notes.D: Parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin and are not the source of T3 or T4 released from follicular colloid.

questions.stem: Why is T3 more biologically potent than T4 at many target cells?
questions.why: Triiodothyronine has greater affinity and functional potency at nuclear thyroid hormone receptors than thyroxine. Much circulating T4 therefore serves as a longer-lived precursor converted within tissues to the more active T3.

notes.B: Thyroxine has a longer circulating half-life than triiodothyronine because of stronger plasma protein binding, despite lower intrinsic receptor potency.
notes.C: The thyroid secretes predominantly thyroxine by quantity; much biologically active triiodothyronine is generated subsequently through peripheral deiodination.
notes.D: Thyroxine is more extensively bound to plasma transport proteins, which prolongs circulation but does not confer greater nuclear receptor activity.
notes.E: Slower cellular entry would not directly explain greater receptor potency; triiodothyronine's stronger interaction with its nuclear receptors is more relevant.

questions.stem: Which enzymes convert much circulating T4 into active T3 in peripheral tissues?
questions.why: Type 1 and type 2 iodothyronine deiodinases remove an outer-ring iodine atom from thyroxine to generate active triiodothyronine. Tissue-specific deiodinase activity regulates local thyroid hormone signalling as well as contributing to circulating T3.

notes.A: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodination and coupling within follicular thyroglobulin, rather than removing iodine from circulating hormone in peripheral tissues.
notes.C: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyses an early step in catecholamine synthesis, rather than converting thyroxine to active triiodothyronine.
notes.D: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylases remove carboxyl groups during neurotransmitter synthesis, rather than selectively removing iodine atoms from iodothyronines.
notes.E: Adrenal steroid hydroxylases modify steroid precursors during corticosteroid synthesis, rather than catalysing peripheral thyroid hormone activation.

questions.stem: High resting oxygen consumption in thyrotoxicosis indicates increased what?
questions.why: Thyroid hormone increases expression and activity of multiple metabolic pathways, including mitochondrial energy metabolism and ATP-consuming processes. Excess hormone therefore increases resting oxygen consumption, heat production and basal energy expenditure in many tissues.

notes.A: Plasma binding proteins influence circulating total hormone concentrations, but increased oxygen consumption indicates enhanced metabolic activity rather than binding alone.
notes.B: Renal phosphate clearance can change in endocrine disorders, but is not the direct explanation for the systemic calorigenic effect of thyroid hormone.
notes.D: Increased oxygen consumption indicates enhanced aerobic metabolism, rather than an isolated increase in anaerobic energy production without oxygen utilisation.
notes.E: Thyroid hormone affects many organ systems; increased resting oxygen consumption reflects broad metabolic stimulation rather than intestinal calcium absorption alone.

questions.stem: Thyroid hormone can lower LDL cholesterol mainly by increasing what?
questions.why: Thyroid hormone increases hepatic LDL receptor expression and promotes receptor-mediated clearance of circulating low-density lipoproteins. Although it also affects cholesterol synthesis and turnover, enhanced clearance can lower plasma LDL cholesterol in hyperthyroid states.

notes.A: Loss of hepatic LDL receptors would impair removal of circulating LDL particles and tend to raise their plasma concentration.
notes.B: Increased intestinal cholesterol synthesis alone does not explain enhanced removal of circulating LDL by the liver under thyroid hormone stimulation.
notes.C: Chylomicrons transport dietary lipids from the intestine, rather than providing the principal mechanism of thyroid hormone-mediated LDL clearance.
notes.E: Inhibition of receptor-mediated LDL endocytosis would reduce particle removal and tend to increase circulating LDL rather than decrease it.

questions.stem: What contributes to tachycardia in a patient with thyroid hormone excess?
questions.why: Excess thyroid hormone increases cardiac responsiveness to adrenergic stimulation and alters expression of proteins regulating pacemaker activity and contraction. These effects contribute to sinus tachycardia and increased cardiac performance, even without markedly increased circulating catecholamine concentrations.

notes.A: Reduced sinoatrial automaticity would slow the heart rate, whereas excess thyroid hormone commonly increases pacemaker activity and produces tachycardia.
notes.B: Reduced catecholamine responsiveness would oppose the characteristic cardiovascular stimulation associated with thyroid hormone excess, rather than explain the faster heart rate.
notes.C: Reduced myocardial beta-adrenergic receptor expression would tend to blunt adrenergic responses, whereas thyroid hormone can enhance cardiac beta-adrenergic signalling.
notes.D: Suppressed cardiac calcium handling would impair aspects of contraction and relaxation, rather than explain the typical hyperdynamic cardiovascular state.

questions.stem: Why can peripheral resistance fall while cardiac output increases in hyperthyroidism?
questions.why: Increased thyroid hormone-driven metabolism generates additional heat and increases tissue metabolic demand, favouring peripheral vasodilatation. Reduced systemic vascular resistance, together with increased heart rate, contractility and circulating volume, contributes to the hyperdynamic circulation of hyperthyroidism.

notes.B: Generalised arteriolar spasm increases vascular resistance and would oppose the vasodilatory haemodynamic pattern commonly observed with excess thyroid hormone.
notes.C: Reduced skin perfusion limits heat loss, whereas hyperthyroidism commonly increases cutaneous blood flow to dissipate excess metabolic heat.
notes.D: Thyroid hormone excess increases rather than reduces metabolic heat production, helping explain compensatory peripheral vasodilatation and heat intolerance.
notes.E: Increased peripheral alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction would raise systemic vascular resistance rather than explain its reduction despite higher cardiac output.

questions.stem: Delayed ankle-jerk relaxation classically suggests which endocrine disturbance?
questions.why: Thyroid hormone deficiency slows skeletal-muscle metabolic and calcium-handling processes, delaying relaxation after contraction. Prolongation of the relaxation phase of deep-tendon reflexes, particularly the ankle jerk, is therefore a classical clinical feature of hypothyroidism.

notes.A: Hyperthyroidism commonly produces brisk reflexes and heightened neuromuscular excitability rather than the characteristically delayed relaxation associated with thyroid deficiency.
notes.C: Aldosterone excess may cause hypokalaemic muscle weakness, but delayed ankle-jerk relaxation is not its characteristic thyroid-like clinical sign.
notes.D: Adrenaline excess produces adrenergic manifestations such as tremor and tachycardia, rather than the classical prolonged relaxation phase of hypothyroid reflexes.
notes.E: Parathyroid hormone excess alters calcium metabolism and may contribute to weakness, but delayed tendon-reflex relaxation is classically associated with hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: Severe congenital hypothyroidism impairs later learning primarily through what?
questions.why: Adequate thyroid hormone is essential during early development for neuronal differentiation, synaptic organisation and myelination. Severe untreated congenital hypothyroidism can disrupt these time-sensitive processes and produce lasting neurodevelopmental impairment, which is why early detection matters.

notes.A: Excess fetal cortical oxygen is not the principal mechanism of neurodevelopmental injury from inadequate thyroid hormone during early life.
notes.B: Thyroid hormone deficiency impairs normal myelination rather than enhancing it, contributing to delayed maturation of the developing nervous system.
notes.D: Fetal steroid synthesis is not the primary thyroid-dependent process accounting for later learning difficulties in severe congenital hypothyroidism.
notes.E: Normal neuronal migration and differentiation require appropriate thyroid hormone signalling; accelerated migration is not the characteristic explanation for developmental impairment.

questions.stem: Free T4 is low and TSH is greatly elevated. Which organ most likely has primary dysfunction?
questions.why: Low free thyroxine reduces negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, increasing thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion. A markedly elevated TSH despite low free T4 therefore indicates failure of the thyroid gland to respond adequately.

notes.A: Primary pituitary failure typically produces low free T4 with an inappropriately low or normal TSH rather than a markedly compensatory elevation.
notes.B: Hypothalamic dysfunction can reduce thyrotropin-releasing hormone drive and cause central hypothyroidism, rather than the usual high-TSH pattern of primary thyroid failure.
notes.C: The pineal gland secretes melatonin and is not the principal organ responsible for thyroid hormone production or pituitary TSH feedback.
notes.E: Adrenal cortical failure affects steroid hormones and can influence other axes, but it does not best explain this characteristic primary thyroid pattern.

questions.stem: Free T4 is low but TSH is inappropriately low. Which disorder best fits?
questions.why: Central hypothyroidism results from insufficient hypothalamic or pituitary stimulation of the thyroid. Free T4 is reduced, but TSH is inappropriately low or normal rather than rising sufficiently to compensate; clinical context helps distinguish pituitary from hypothalamic disease.

notes.A: Primary hypothyroidism generally causes a compensatory increase in TSH because the pituitary senses inadequate circulating thyroid hormone and increases stimulation.
notes.B: Graves disease usually produces excess thyroid hormone through stimulatory TSH-receptor antibodies, resulting in elevated free hormone and suppressed endogenous TSH.
notes.C: Toxic nodular hyperthyroidism causes autonomous thyroid hormone production, typically increasing circulating hormone concentrations while suppressing pituitary TSH through feedback.
notes.D: Thyroid hormone resistance commonly presents with elevated thyroid hormone concentrations and inadequately suppressed TSH, rather than this low-free-T4 central pattern.

questions.stem: Yellow skin without yellow sclerae in hypothyroidism may reflect what?
questions.why: Hypothyroidism can reduce conversion of beta-carotene to vitamin A, allowing carotene to accumulate in skin and produce yellow-orange discoloration. Unlike jaundice, carotenemia typically spares the sclerae.

notes.B: Bilirubin accumulation causes jaundice and commonly discolours the sclerae as well as skin, unlike the described distribution.
notes.C: Melanin accumulation produces brown or darker pigmentation rather than the characteristic yellow-orange discoloration from excess carotene.
notes.D: Haemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin and may produce scleral icterus, rather than isolated yellow skin with spared sclerae.
notes.E: Hypothyroidism commonly reduces LDL clearance and raises cholesterol; decreased cholesterol does not explain the yellow skin.

questions.stem: What explains short stature with longstanding childhood hypothyroidism?
questions.why: Thyroid hormone is necessary for normal growth-plate maturation and skeletal development. Prolonged childhood deficiency delays bone age, reduces growth velocity and impairs GH–IGF-1-dependent growth, producing short stature.

notes.A: Thyroid deficiency generally delays rather than accelerates growth-plate maturation, so premature epiphyseal fusion is not the principal mechanism.
notes.C: Excess longitudinal bone growth would increase stature rather than explain the reduced growth velocity of longstanding childhood hypothyroidism.
notes.D: Altered cortical remodelling may accompany thyroid disorders, but delayed skeletal maturation better explains impaired linear growth in childhood deficiency.
notes.E: Accelerated epiphyseal growth would favour increased linear growth, whereas thyroid deficiency impairs normal growth-plate development and maturation.

questions.stem: A patient has heat intolerance, tremor and raised free T4. Which TSH level suggests primary hyperthyroidism?
questions.why: In primary hyperthyroidism, the thyroid produces excessive hormone independently of normal pituitary demand. Elevated free T4 and T3 suppress hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH through negative feedback, explaining the low TSH.

notes.A: Elevated TSH despite high free T4 suggests an inappropriate central response, such as a TSH-secreting adenoma, rather than ordinary primary hyperthyroidism.
notes.B: ACTH regulates adrenal cortisol production and is not the pituitary hormone used to identify primary thyroid hormone excess.
notes.D: Prolactin regulates lactation and can change in selected thyroid disorders, but it is not the principal feedback marker of hyperthyroidism.
notes.E: Thyroid hormone excess suppresses hypothalamic TRH through negative feedback, rather than normally increasing hypothalamic stimulation of the thyroid axis.

questions.stem: Extracellular calcium entering a presynaptic terminal triggers which event?
questions.why: An arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic membrane. Calcium binds release-sensing proteins such as synaptotagmin, triggering synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.

notes.A: Myelin is produced by specialised glial cells, whereas rapid presynaptic calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion within the neuronal terminal.
notes.B: Oxygen binding to haemoglobin occurs at ferrous haem groups and is unrelated to the calcium-dependent synaptic release mechanism.
notes.C: DNA base pairing supports genetic information storage and replication, rather than mediating rapid chemical transmission across a synaptic cleft.
notes.E: Glycogen branching is an enzymatic carbohydrate-storage process, rather than the immediate consequence of calcium entry into an activated presynaptic terminal.

questions.stem: Why does severe hypocalcaemia cause tetany and muscle spasms?
questions.why: Reduced extracellular ionised calcium makes voltage-gated sodium channels easier to activate and lowers the threshold for action potential initiation. Increased spontaneous neuronal firing and neuromuscular excitability can consequently produce paraesthesiae, cramps and tetany.

notes.A: Decreased neuronal excitability would suppress spontaneous discharge and muscle spasms, whereas significant hypocalcaemia characteristically increases neuromuscular excitability.
notes.B: Reduced sodium channel activation would usually impede depolarisation; low extracellular calcium instead facilitates activation of excitatory membrane conductances.
notes.C: Enhanced neural inhibition would reduce motor activity rather than explain the spontaneous muscle contractions associated with reduced ionised calcium.
notes.D: Reduced skeletal neuromuscular excitability is more consistent with significant hypercalcaemia, whereas hypocalcaemia can produce tetanic contractions.

questions.stem: Carpal spasm after inflation of a blood-pressure cuff demonstrates which sign?
questions.why: Trousseau sign is carpal spasm elicited by maintaining blood-pressure cuff inflation above systolic pressure for several minutes. It demonstrates latent neuromuscular hyperexcitability, commonly associated with reduced ionised calcium, although other disturbances can also produce it.

notes.B: Chvostek sign is facial muscle twitching elicited by tapping over the facial nerve, rather than cuff-induced carpal spasm.
notes.C: Babinski sign is extension of the great toe after plantar stimulation, suggesting corticospinal tract dysfunction in adults.
notes.D: Romberg testing assesses the contribution of proprioceptive and vestibular input to standing balance, rather than latent hypocalcaemic tetany.
notes.E: Hoffmann sign involves reflex finger or thumb flexion after stimulation of a finger, rather than sustained carpal spasm after cuff inflation.

questions.stem: Tapping the facial nerve produces twitching of facial muscles. Which sign is this?
questions.why: Chvostek sign is contraction of facial muscles after tapping the facial nerve near its superficial course. It reflects increased nerve excitability and can occur in hypocalcaemia, but is not sufficiently specific to diagnose calcium deficiency alone.

notes.A: Trousseau sign is provoked by prolonged blood-pressure cuff inflation and produces carpal spasm rather than facial muscle twitching.
notes.C: Kernig sign describes resistance or pain with knee extension when the hip is flexed, classically associated with meningeal irritation.
notes.D: Brudzinski sign involves involuntary hip and knee flexion during passive neck flexion, rather than direct stimulation of the facial nerve.
notes.E: Lhermitte sign is an electric shock-like sensation with neck movement, commonly associated with cervical spinal cord pathology.

questions.stem: A hyperventilating patient develops tetany with normal total plasma calcium. What changed?
questions.why: Hyperventilation reduces arterial carbon dioxide and produces respiratory alkalosis. Higher pH increases albumin binding of calcium, decreasing physiologically active ionised calcium despite unchanged total calcium concentration and increasing neuromuscular excitability.

notes.A: Acidosis generally decreases albumin calcium binding and increases the ionised fraction, rather than explaining tetany after hyperventilation.
notes.B: Respiratory alkalosis primarily changes the distribution between bound and ionised calcium, rather than necessarily increasing total plasma calcium.
notes.D: Acidosis can increase ionised calcium, but hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide and produces alkalosis rather than the stated acidic disturbance.
notes.E: Changes in free magnesium do not best explain this classic presentation; reduced ionised calcium increases neuromuscular excitability.

questions.stem: Which neurological finding is expected with significant hypercalcaemia?
questions.why: High extracellular calcium increases the threshold for activation of excitable membranes, reducing neuromuscular responsiveness. Significant hypercalcaemia may therefore cause weakness, lethargy and diminished tendon reflexes, contrasting with the tetany of hypocalcaemia.

notes.A: Carpopedal spasm is characteristic of increased neuromuscular excitability, commonly from reduced rather than increased ionised calcium.
notes.B: Repetitive clonic seizures are more characteristic of severe hypocalcaemic hyperexcitability, although many metabolic disturbances may cause seizures.
notes.C: Raised neuronal excitability is the classic effect of reduced extracellular calcium, whereas hypercalcaemia generally depresses neuromuscular responsiveness.
notes.E: Latent tetany reflects increased nerve and muscle excitability and is more commonly associated with hypocalcaemia or alkalosis.

questions.stem: Which bone cell primarily secretes collagen-rich osteoid for mineralization?
questions.why: Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells that secrete osteoid, an organic matrix rich in type I collagen and non-collagenous proteins. Subsequent mineral deposition within this matrix produces mechanically strong mature bone.

notes.A: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells that resorb mineralised bone through acidification and proteolysis rather than secreting new osteoid.
notes.B: Osteocytes are mature embedded bone cells that sense mechanical loading and regulate remodelling, rather than being the principal osteoid-secreting population.
notes.C: Chondroclasts resorb mineralised cartilage during skeletal development and do not provide the principal source of new bone matrix.
notes.D: Chondrocytes produce cartilage matrix, which differs from the type I collagen-rich osteoid deposited by bone-forming osteoblasts.

questions.stem: Severely reduced osteoclast activity can produce which bone disorder?
questions.why: Osteoclasts remove mineralised bone during normal remodelling. Severe impairment of their development or resorptive function causes osteopetrosis, characterised by excessively dense but often brittle bones and possible reduction of marrow space.

notes.B: Osteoporosis involves reduced bone mass and disrupted microarchitecture, commonly reflecting an imbalance favouring resorption rather than severely impaired osteoclast function.
notes.C: Osteomalacia results from inadequate mineralisation of newly deposited adult bone matrix, rather than failure to resorb existing mineralised bone.
notes.D: Rickets involves defective mineralisation at growing skeletal growth plates, rather than excessive retention of bone from impaired resorption.
notes.E: Osteomyelitis is infection and inflammation of bone, rather than an inherited or acquired failure of osteoclastic bone resorption.

questions.stem: Which constituent provides most resistance to compression in healthy bone?
questions.why: Hydroxyapatite crystals provide bone with hardness and resistance to compressive forces. Type I collagen contributes tensile strength and toughness, while their organised combination creates a composite tissue resistant to multiple forms of mechanical loading.

notes.A: Type I collagen provides tensile strength and flexibility, rather than the major compressive rigidity contributed by inorganic mineral crystals.
notes.C: Unmineralised osteoid is the organic precursor of bone and lacks much of the compressive stiffness provided by deposited mineral.
notes.D: Cartilage proteoglycans resist compression within hydrated cartilage, but mineralised bone chiefly gains compressive rigidity from hydroxyapatite.
notes.E: Elastic fibres support recoil in specialised connective tissues and are not the principal load-bearing mineral component of normal bone.

questions.stem: A vitamin D-deficient child has bowed legs and poor bone mineralization. Which condition is most likely?
questions.why: Vitamin D deficiency reduces efficient intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and can impair mineralisation of growing bone and growth plates. This produces rickets, with skeletal deformities such as bowed legs under weight-bearing forces.

notes.A: Osteoporosis is reduced bone mass with relatively normal mineralisation of remaining matrix, rather than the characteristic growth-plate mineralisation defect in children.
notes.B: Osteopetrosis causes abnormally dense bone through impaired osteoclastic resorption, rather than vitamin D-related failure of mineral deposition.
notes.D: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone, typically associated with inflammatory features rather than the characteristic nutritional growth-plate abnormality.
notes.E: Osteogenesis imperfecta usually involves defects in type I collagen and bone fragility, rather than acquired vitamin D-deficient growth-plate mineralisation.

questions.stem: Which contrast best separates osteoporosis from osteomalacia?

options.label: A
options.text: Too much collagen versus low calcium

options.label: D
options.text: Less bone mass versus poor mineralization

questions.why: Osteoporosis involves reduced bone quantity and deterioration of microarchitecture, with relatively preserved mineralisation of remaining matrix. Osteomalacia instead involves defective mineralisation of osteoid, leaving excess unmineralised matrix despite ongoing bone formation.

notes.A: Excess collagen is not the defining feature of osteoporosis, and serum calcium may remain normal in osteomalacia despite impaired mineralisation.
notes.B: Osteoclast activity and phosphate deficiency can contribute to these conditions, but neither pairing defines their fundamental structural difference.
notes.C: Calcitonin excess and PTH deficiency do not define the two disorders; the key distinction is bone quantity versus mineralisation quality.
notes.E: Reduced marrow space is more characteristic of osteopetrosis, while excess unmineralised osteoid characterises osteomalacia but does not identify osteoporosis.

questions.stem: Where does the final hydroxylation yielding calcitriol mainly occur?
questions.why: Renal proximal tubular cells express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts liver-derived 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol. This final major activation step is regulated by PTH, phosphate-related signals and feedback from active vitamin D.

notes.A: Hepatocytes carry out the earlier 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D, rather than the main regulated final activation to calcitriol.
notes.B: Thyroid follicular cells synthesise thyroid hormones through iodination of thyroglobulin and are not the principal site of calcitriol activation.
notes.C: Adrenal medullary cells produce catecholamines and do not account for the main endocrine production of active vitamin D.
notes.D: Intestinal mucosa responds to calcitriol by increasing mineral absorption, rather than serving as its primary regulated systemic production site.

questions.stem: Which endocrine signal increases the kidney's production of active vitamin D?
questions.why: Parathyroid hormone increases renal proximal tubular 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, promoting conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol. This response supports calcium homeostasis by increasing intestinal mineral absorption during conditions such as reduced circulating ionised calcium.

notes.B: Calcitonin principally inhibits osteoclast-mediated resorption and is not the main physiological stimulus driving renal calcitriol production during hypocalcaemia.
notes.C: Glucagon regulates hepatic glucose production during fasting and does not provide the principal calcium-regulated stimulus to renal vitamin D activation.
notes.D: TSH stimulates thyroid follicular hormone synthesis and release, rather than regulating the renal enzyme that activates vitamin D.
notes.E: Adrenaline mediates acute sympathetic metabolic responses, whereas renal calcitriol production is stimulated chiefly by PTH and mineral-related regulatory signals.

questions.stem: Calcitriol improves calcium balance primarily through which gut effect?
questions.why: Calcitriol activates intestinal vitamin D receptors, increasing expression of proteins involved in transcellular calcium entry, intracellular handling and basolateral export. Enhanced calcium absorption helps maintain extracellular calcium concentration and supplies mineral for normal skeletal mineralisation.

notes.A: Reduced intestinal calcium transport would impair calcium acquisition, whereas calcitriol increases the capacity for active intestinal calcium absorption.
notes.C: Renal calcium handling can be influenced by calcitriol, but increased renal secretion is neither its principal gut action nor a calcium-conserving mechanism.
notes.D: Calcitriol generally supports normal bone mineralisation by improving mineral availability, although its skeletal actions depend on physiological context.
notes.E: Urinary phosphate excretion is regulated strongly by PTH and FGF23; calcitriol's specified intestinal effect is enhanced calcium uptake.

questions.stem: Why can serum phosphate fall in primary hyperparathyroidism despite bone resorption?
questions.why: PTH reduces expression of sodium–phosphate cotransporters in proximal tubular cells, decreasing renal phosphate reabsorption and increasing urinary phosphate loss. This phosphaturic effect can outweigh phosphate released from bone, lowering serum phosphate in primary hyperparathyroidism.

notes.A: Increased renal phosphate reabsorption would favour phosphate retention and oppose the characteristic phosphaturic response to excess PTH.
notes.B: PTH-stimulated calcitriol can enhance intestinal phosphate absorption; the low serum phosphate is explained primarily by renal phosphate wasting.
notes.D: Bone resorption may increase under sustained PTH exposure, so complete suppression of skeletal phosphate release is not the usual explanation.
notes.E: Calcitonin is not the principal mediator of the renal phosphate loss characteristic of primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH directly alters proximal tubular transport.

questions.stem: How do chief cells respond immediately when plasma ionized calcium falls?
questions.why: Parathyroid chief cells detect extracellular ionised calcium through the calcium-sensing receptor. Falling calcium reduces inhibitory receptor signalling and rapidly increases PTH secretion, initiating responses that conserve calcium and restore its circulating concentration.

notes.A: Reduced PTH secretion would oppose calcium recovery and is more characteristic of increased extracellular calcium activating the calcium-sensing receptor.
notes.B: Calcitonin is released from thyroid parafollicular cells, chiefly in response to increased calcium, rather than from parathyroid chief cells.
notes.C: PTH stimulates renal calcitriol production during calcium deficiency, so reduced calcitriol formation is not the normal compensatory response.
notes.E: Increased skeletal mineral deposition alone would consume circulating calcium, whereas the immediate chief-cell response is increased hormone secretion.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern follows complete loss of parathyroid hormone secretion?
questions.why: Loss of PTH reduces renal calcium conservation and calcitriol synthesis while removing its inhibitory effect on proximal phosphate reabsorption. Consequently, circulating calcium tends to fall and phosphate tends to rise, producing the characteristic hypoparathyroid pattern.

notes.A: High calcium with low phosphate is more typical of excessive PTH activity, rather than complete absence of its secretion.
notes.B: High calcium is not the expected direct consequence of PTH loss, despite increased phosphate retention from reduced phosphaturic signalling.
notes.C: Low calcium is expected, but phosphate generally rises because the kidney no longer receives normal PTH-mediated phosphaturic stimulation.
notes.D: Normal calcium with low phosphate does not reflect the combined reduction in calcium-conserving actions and phosphate excretion following PTH loss.

questions.stem: Calcitonin lowers circulating calcium by which direct action?
questions.why: Calcitonin released from thyroid parafollicular cells binds receptors on osteoclasts and suppresses their bone-resorbing activity. This reduces calcium release from mineralised bone, although calcitonin has a relatively limited role in long-term calcium homeostasis in adults.

notes.B: Stimulating osteoclast activity would increase calcium release from bone, opposing the principal calcium-lowering action of calcitonin.
notes.C: Enhanced intestinal calcium absorption would increase calcium availability and is chiefly associated with calcitriol rather than calcitonin's direct skeletal action.
notes.D: Increased renal calcium retention would conserve circulating calcium rather than explain the calcium-lowering effect produced by osteoclast inhibition.
notes.E: Increased calcitriol production generally supports intestinal calcium uptake and is primarily stimulated by PTH rather than calcitonin acting on bone.

questions.stem: A lesion confined to the zona glomerulosa primarily changes secretion of which hormone?
questions.why: The zona glomerulosa is the outer adrenal cortical layer and expresses aldosterone synthase, enabling mineralocorticoid production. Its secretion is regulated predominantly by angiotensin II and extracellular potassium, supporting sodium and potassium balance.

notes.A: Cortisol is produced mainly by the zona fasciculata under ACTH regulation, rather than the mineralocorticoid-producing zona glomerulosa.
notes.C: Dehydroepiandrosterone is an adrenal androgen precursor produced predominantly in the zona reticularis, rather than the outer cortical layer.
notes.D: Adrenaline is synthesised by adrenal medullary chromaffin cells, which are anatomically distinct from the outer adrenal cortex.
notes.E: Noradrenaline is a catecholamine produced by medullary chromaffin cells and sympathetic neurons, rather than the principal product of zona glomerulosa.

questions.stem: Which adrenal layer produces most circulating cortisol in a healthy adult?
questions.why: The zona fasciculata forms the thick middle adrenal cortical layer and contains the enzymes required for glucocorticoid synthesis. ACTH stimulates its steroidogenic activity, making it the principal source of circulating cortisol in healthy adults.

notes.A: The zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone and lacks the normal enzyme complement required for the major cortisol synthesis pathway.
notes.B: The zona reticularis produces predominantly adrenal androgen precursors, although some glucocorticoid synthesis can occur in inner cortical cells.
notes.D: The adrenal medulla produces catecholamines in response to sympathetic stimulation and does not synthesise most circulating cortisol.
notes.E: The adrenal capsule is a connective-tissue covering rather than a differentiated steroidogenic zone responsible for systemic cortisol production.

questions.stem: Selective loss of zona reticularis activity most directly decreases what?
questions.why: The zona reticularis is the innermost adrenal cortical layer and preferentially produces androgen precursors including DHEA and DHEA sulphate. Reduced activity therefore primarily lowers adrenal androgen output, with potential effects on androgen-dependent tissues.

notes.A: Adrenaline production occurs in chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, not principally in the androgen-producing zona reticularis.
notes.B: Aldosterone synthesis occurs predominantly in the zona glomerulosa, so a selective reticularis lesion does not directly remove its main source.
notes.C: Thyroxine is synthesised by thyroid follicular cells and is not an adrenal cortical steroid product.
notes.E: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin independently of direct steroid synthesis in the adrenal zona reticularis.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal regulatory axis?
questions.why: Hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone stimulates anterior pituitary corticotrophs to release ACTH. ACTH activates adrenal cortical cortisol synthesis, and circulating cortisol feeds back on both hypothalamus and pituitary to regulate the stress axis.

notes.A: TRH stimulates TSH release and thyroid hormone production, rather than forming the principal hypothalamic–pituitary pathway controlling cortisol.
notes.B: GnRH stimulates gonadotropin secretion and gonadal steroid production, rather than providing the direct pituitary stimulus to adrenal cortisol synthesis.
notes.C: GHRH promotes growth hormone secretion and downstream IGF-1 signalling, whereas adrenal cortisol production is predominantly controlled by ACTH.
notes.D: CRH stimulates corticotrophs to release ACTH rather than thyrotrophs releasing TSH, which regulates thyroid hormone synthesis.

questions.stem: Why can abrupt withdrawal of prolonged high-dose glucocorticoids cause adrenal insufficiency?
questions.why: Prolonged exogenous glucocorticoid exposure suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH through negative feedback. Reduced trophic ACTH stimulation can cause adrenal cortical atrophy, leaving insufficient endogenous cortisol production when treatment is withdrawn abruptly.

notes.B: The principal suppression concerns adrenal cortical glucocorticoid production, rather than acute destruction of catecholamine-producing adrenal medullary cells.
notes.C: Glucocorticoid treatment suppresses the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis without necessarily destroying mineralocorticoid receptors or abolishing their responsiveness.
notes.D: Renin–angiotensin signalling often remains relatively preserved in secondary adrenal suppression; chronic ACTH deficiency explains impaired cortisol production.
notes.E: Thyroid hormone receptors regulate a separate endocrine pathway and their loss is not the mechanism of glucocorticoid withdrawal-associated adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: Which hepatic metabolic process is enhanced by cortisol during prolonged fasting?
questions.why: Cortisol supports fasting glucose availability by increasing hepatic expression of gluconeogenic enzymes and mobilising amino acid and other metabolic substrates. It also opposes some peripheral insulin actions, helping preserve circulating glucose during prolonged nutritional deprivation.

notes.A: Glucose uptake into peripheral tissues may decrease under cortisol influence; increased hepatic glucose production rather than uptake is the relevant fasting response.
notes.C: Cortisol influences glycogen metabolism, but inhibition of glycogenolysis alone does not explain generation of glucose from non-carbohydrate substrates.
notes.D: Lipid metabolism is also affected by cortisol, but exclusive triglyceride synthesis does not account for its role in maintaining fasting glucose.
notes.E: Glucose oxidation consumes glucose, whereas cortisol promotes production of glucose through hepatic gluconeogenesis during fasting.

questions.stem: Long-term glucocorticoid treatment causes easy bruising and delayed wound healing. Why?
questions.why: Excess glucocorticoid signalling suppresses fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis while modifying inflammatory and repair responses. Reduced connective-tissue integrity makes skin and superficial vessels fragile, contributing to easy bruising, striae and delayed wound healing.

notes.A: Increased collagen deposition would generally strengthen connective tissue rather than explain glucocorticoid-associated thinning and fragility of skin.
notes.B: Glucocorticoids suppress rather than promote many fibroblast proliferative and matrix-synthetic responses required for normal tissue repair.
notes.D: Enhanced capillary and surrounding tissue strength would reduce bruising; glucocorticoid-related connective-tissue loss increases susceptibility to injury.
notes.E: Increased elastin production is not the main established mechanism of glucocorticoid-impaired repair, which involves suppressed matrix synthesis and cellular proliferation.

questions.stem: What mechanism helps explain steroid-induced osteoporosis?
questions.why: Prolonged glucocorticoid excess suppresses osteoblast differentiation and bone formation, increases osteoblast and osteocyte loss, and can impair calcium balance. Early increases in resorption and persistent reduction in formation contribute to glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.

notes.A: Enhanced osteoblast proliferation would support bone formation, whereas glucocorticoid excess characteristically suppresses osteoblast function and survival.
notes.B: Glucocorticoids can reduce intestinal calcium absorption, rather than increasing it as a protective mechanism against bone loss.
notes.C: Increased synthesis of bone collagen would favour osteoid production, but prolonged glucocorticoid exposure generally reduces osteoblast-dependent matrix formation.
notes.E: Complete blockade of osteoclasts would impair resorption; glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis involves altered remodelling and particularly reduced bone formation.

questions.stem: Why can severe glucocorticoid deficiency produce hypotension during acute stress?
questions.why: Cortisol has permissive effects on vascular responses to catecholamines and other pressor signals. Severe deficiency can reduce vascular tone and responsiveness during stress, contributing to hypotension, especially when concurrent mineralocorticoid deficiency causes volume depletion.

notes.A: Enhanced vascular alpha-adrenergic sensitivity would support vasoconstriction and arterial pressure rather than explain the impaired pressor response of cortisol deficiency.
notes.B: Excess renal sodium retention would support extracellular volume; primary adrenal insufficiency may instead cause sodium loss through aldosterone deficiency.
notes.C: Enhanced cardiac beta-adrenergic activity could support cardiac performance, but loss of cortisol reduces normal responsiveness to stress-related catecholamine signals.
notes.D: Angiotensin II may increase compensatorily during reduced perfusion, but its pressor action does not directly explain the hypotension caused by impaired vascular responsiveness.

questions.stem: A patient has low BP, hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperpigmentation. What is most likely?
questions.why: Primary adrenal cortical failure reduces cortisol and often aldosterone secretion. Mineralocorticoid deficiency causes sodium loss and potassium retention, while loss of cortisol feedback raises ACTH and melanocortin signalling, explaining hypotension and hyperpigmentation.

notes.B: Secondary adrenal insufficiency usually preserves aldosterone and does not produce marked ACTH-driven pigmentation, although cortisol deficiency can cause hyponatraemia.
notes.C: Primary hyperaldosteronism typically causes hypertension and sometimes hypokalaemia, rather than the low-pressure hyperkalaemic pattern of mineralocorticoid deficiency.
notes.D: An ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour usually causes cortisol excess and Cushing disease, rather than primary adrenal failure with combined steroid deficiency.
notes.E: Adrenal medullary hyperfunction produces catecholamine-related manifestations such as episodic hypertension and sweating, rather than this combined cortical hormone-deficiency pattern.

questions.stem: A patient has low cortisol but preserved aldosterone and no hyperpigmentation. What defect is most likely?
questions.why: Pituitary ACTH deficiency reduces cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata while usually preserving aldosterone regulation through angiotensin II and potassium. Low or inappropriately normal ACTH also avoids the marked melanocortin stimulation characteristic of primary adrenal failure.

notes.A: Bilateral adrenal destruction can impair both cortisol and aldosterone production and usually increases ACTH through loss of negative feedback.
notes.C: Selective glomerulosa failure primarily decreases aldosterone while preserving cortisol production from other cortical zones, opposite to the pattern described.
notes.D: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage can cause primary adrenal insufficiency involving multiple cortical hormone pathways and compensatory ACTH elevation.
notes.E: Congenital aldosterone deficiency primarily impairs mineralocorticoid production rather than selectively reducing cortisol while maintaining aldosterone.

questions.stem: Aldosterone has which direct effect on the late distal nephron?
questions.why: Aldosterone activates mineralocorticoid receptors in late distal nephron principal cells, increasing epithelial sodium channel activity and basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase. Enhanced sodium reabsorption commonly facilitates potassium secretion and supports extracellular fluid volume.

notes.A: Increased urinary sodium excretion is a natriuretic response, whereas aldosterone generally promotes sodium conservation in responsive distal tubular cells.
notes.B: Aldosterone commonly increases potassium secretion through changes in sodium transport and potassium-channel activity, rather than suppressing it.
notes.D: Aldosterone can enhance distal hydrogen ion secretion through intercalated-cell mechanisms, rather than characteristically decreasing renal acid secretion.
notes.E: Aldosterone increases the expression and activity of epithelial sodium channels, while drugs such as amiloride block those channels.

questions.stem: Hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis suggest excess secretion of what?
questions.why: Excess aldosterone increases distal sodium reabsorption and promotes potassium and hydrogen ion secretion. Sodium retention can expand extracellular volume and cause hypertension, while increased potassium and acid loss may produce hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.

notes.A: Vasopressin primarily conserves water through collecting-duct aquaporins and does not characteristically produce the combined potassium-wasting alkalotic pattern.
notes.B: Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast activity and influences calcium metabolism, rather than being the main hormone responsible for distal sodium retention and potassium loss.
notes.C: Somatostatin inhibits several endocrine and gastrointestinal secretions, but does not produce the characteristic mineralocorticoid pattern of electrolyte disturbances.
notes.E: Thyroxine excess can increase cardiovascular activity, but it does not directly explain the combination of potassium wasting and metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: Renin release in response to poor renal perfusion originates mainly from which cells?
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular granular cells are modified arteriolar smooth-muscle cells, located mainly in the afferent arteriole near the renal corpuscle. Reduced perfusion pressure, beta-1 stimulation and low macula densa sodium chloride delivery promote renin secretion.

notes.A: Proximal tubular epithelial cells perform extensive solute reabsorption and vitamin D activation, rather than serving as the principal renin-releasing cells.
notes.B: Chromaffin cells release catecholamines from the adrenal medulla and are not the main source of renal renin.
notes.C: Podocytes provide filtration slit structures within renal corpuscles, rather than secreting renin in response to reduced renal perfusion.
notes.D: Collecting-duct principal cells regulate distal sodium, potassium and water handling, rather than supplying the principal circulating renin response.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II in the circulation?
questions.why: Angiotensin-converting enzyme removes a terminal dipeptide from angiotensin I to form the active octapeptide angiotensin II. ACE is expressed on vascular endothelial surfaces, prominently in pulmonary vessels, and also contributes to bradykinin degradation.

notes.B: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to produce angiotensin I, rather than catalysing the subsequent conversion to active angiotensin II.
notes.C: Aldosterone synthase catalyses final steroidogenic steps in zona glomerulosa cells, rather than processing circulating angiotensin peptides.
notes.D: Adrenal 11-beta-hydroxylase participates in cortisol and corticosterone synthesis, not the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
notes.E: Aromatase converts androgen precursors into oestrogens, rather than acting as a peptide-cleaving enzyme in the renin–angiotensin system.

questions.stem: Which disturbance directly promotes aldosterone secretion independent of ACTH?
questions.why: Raised extracellular potassium depolarises zona glomerulosa cells, increasing calcium entry and steroidogenic signalling. This directly stimulates aldosterone synthesis independently of pituitary ACTH, promoting renal potassium excretion and helping restore potassium balance.

notes.A: Reduced extracellular potassium generally decreases aldosterone stimulation, thereby limiting further potassium loss rather than provoking increased mineralocorticoid secretion.
notes.C: Elevated plasma sodium is not the principal direct glomerulosa stimulus; potassium and angiotensin II dominate physiological aldosterone regulation.
notes.D: Reduced angiotensin II removes an important stimulatory signal for aldosterone synthesis, rather than directly increasing its secretion.
notes.E: Reduced renal renin output generally decreases angiotensin II formation and consequently reduces renin–angiotensin-dependent stimulation of aldosterone.

questions.stem: What directly stimulates chromaffin cells during an acute sympathetic response?
questions.why: Adrenal chromaffin cells receive acetylcholine from sympathetic preganglionic fibres travelling through splanchnic nerves. Activation of nicotinic receptors depolarises the cells, increases intracellular calcium and triggers rapid exocytosis of stored catecholamines.

notes.A: The adrenal medulla is innervated by sympathetic preganglionic fibres, rather than by postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor neurons.
notes.B: Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary and is not the principal direct signal causing acute adrenal catecholamine secretion.
notes.D: Adrenal cortical cortisol supports adrenaline synthesis by inducing PNMT, but rapid chromaffin-cell exocytosis is triggered chiefly by neural acetylcholine.
notes.E: Angiotensin I is a renin-generated precursor peptide, rather than the immediate neurotransmitter released onto chromaffin cells during sympathetic activation.

questions.stem: A patient has episodic sweating, severe headaches and hypertension. Which investigation supports a medullary tumour?
questions.why: Phaeochromocytomas arise from chromaffin cells and may produce catecholamine-related episodes of headache, sweating and hypertension. Plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines detect their metabolites, which can be produced continuously even between secretory episodes.

notes.A: Reduced urinary catecholamines do not support excessive catecholamine production, although tumour secretion and measured concentrations can vary with sampling conditions.
