notes.B: Catecholamine excess commonly increases hepatic glucose output and can raise blood glucose, rather than characteristically causing persistent hypoglycaemia.
notes.C: Absent circulating adrenaline would not support a catecholamine-producing tumour, although individual tumours differ in the catecholamines they predominantly produce.
notes.E: Low urinary catecholamine metabolites do not provide positive biochemical evidence of a chromaffin tumour; elevated fractionated metanephrines are more informative.

questions.stem: At modest concentrations, adrenaline dilates arterioles in skeletal muscle through which receptor?
questions.why: At relatively modest concentrations, adrenaline can activate beta-2 adrenergic receptors in skeletal-muscle vascular smooth muscle. Gs-dependent cAMP signalling promotes relaxation, producing vasodilatation that can oppose alpha-mediated constriction depending on local receptor balance.

notes.A: Alpha-1 receptor activation increases vascular smooth-muscle calcium signalling and generally causes vasoconstriction rather than the described adrenergic relaxation.
notes.B: Muscarinic M3 signalling can stimulate endothelial nitric oxide release in some vessels, but adrenaline does not act as its physiological agonist.
notes.C: Angiotensin AT1 receptors mediate many vasoconstrictor actions of angiotensin II, rather than adrenaline-induced skeletal muscle vasodilatation.
notes.D: Vasopressin V1 receptors promote vascular smooth-muscle contraction, whereas adrenaline-mediated relaxation in this setting principally involves beta-2 receptors.

questions.stem: What is a characteristic cardiac effect of beta-1 receptor stimulation?
questions.why: Cardiac beta-1 receptor activation stimulates Gs-dependent cAMP and protein kinase A signalling, enhancing calcium entry and sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release. Increased calcium availability strengthens myocardial contraction and also supports faster pacemaker firing and conduction.

notes.B: Beta-1 stimulation generally accelerates atrioventricular nodal conduction, whereas reduced conduction speed is more characteristic of parasympathetic influence.
notes.C: Sinoatrial beta-1 activation increases pacemaker depolarisation and heart rate, rather than reducing the frequency of spontaneous firing.
notes.D: Beta-1 signalling enhances calcium handling, including L-type calcium entry, rather than reducing the calcium transient responsible for contraction.
notes.E: Beta-1 receptors activate adenylyl cyclase through Gs proteins, increasing myocardial cAMP rather than lowering its intracellular concentration.

questions.stem: A patient develops truncal fat gain, wide purple striae and proximal weakness. Which process explains the weakness?
questions.why: Chronic cortisol excess increases skeletal muscle protein catabolism and inhibits anabolic processes, releasing amino acid substrates for hepatic gluconeogenesis. Loss of muscle protein and atrophy, particularly in proximal muscles, contribute to the characteristic glucocorticoid myopathy.

notes.A: Cortisol promotes hepatic glucose production, but reduced hepatic glucose output does not explain the proximal loss of muscle strength.
notes.C: Reduced protein degradation would tend to preserve muscle mass, whereas sustained glucocorticoid excess promotes net skeletal muscle protein loss.
notes.D: Increased muscle protein synthesis would oppose atrophy; glucocorticoid excess generally reduces anabolic signalling while promoting protein catabolism.
notes.E: Cortisol can oppose insulin-mediated peripheral glucose uptake, but increased glucose uptake is not the principal mechanism of glucocorticoid-induced proximal weakness.

questions.stem: An ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma leads to cortisol excess. What is this specifically called?
questions.why: Cushing disease specifically denotes cortisol excess caused by a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma. It is one cause of Cushing syndrome, the broader clinical state of glucocorticoid excess arising from endogenous or exogenous sources.

notes.A: Addison disease describes primary adrenal insufficiency, which produces deficient rather than excessive cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex.
notes.B: Conn syndrome classically refers to primary hyperaldosteronism, a mineralocorticoid excess disorder distinct from ACTH-dependent cortisol excess.
notes.D: Nelson syndrome involves progression of a corticotroph tumour after bilateral adrenalectomy, rather than the general name for pituitary-driven Cushing syndrome.
notes.E: Phaeochromocytoma is a chromaffin-cell tumour that produces catecholamines rather than a pituitary corticotroph adenoma causing cortisol excess.

questions.stem: Which islet cells release somatostatin that locally inhibits other islet hormones?
questions.why: Pancreatic islet delta cells release somatostatin, which acts locally on neighbouring endocrine cells through inhibitory somatostatin receptors. This paracrine signalling restrains insulin and glucagon release, helping coordinate the islet response to nutrient and hormonal signals.

notes.A: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises hepatic glucose output and is regulated partly by somatostatin from neighbouring delta cells.
notes.B: Beta cells produce insulin and amylin, rather than serving as the main source of inhibitory islet somatostatin.
notes.C: PP cells produce pancreatic polypeptide, which influences gastrointestinal and pancreatic function, rather than releasing the principal local islet somatostatin.
notes.E: Acinar cells are exocrine pancreatic cells that secrete digestive enzymes into ducts, rather than providing the main endocrine source of somatostatin.

questions.stem: Which endocrine cell type releases pancreatic polypeptide?
questions.why: Pancreatic polypeptide is secreted by specialised islet PP cells, also called F or gamma cells. These cells are particularly abundant in parts of the pancreatic head and their hormone participates in regulation of pancreatic and gastrointestinal function.

notes.A: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which acts mainly to support glucose availability during fasting, rather than secreting pancreatic polypeptide.
notes.B: Beta cells synthesise insulin and amylin in response to metabolic signals, rather than being the principal source of pancreatic polypeptide.
notes.C: Delta cells produce somatostatin, which inhibits several nearby islet hormone secretions, rather than producing pancreatic polypeptide.
notes.D: Exocrine acinar and ductal cells produce digestive enzymes and bicarbonate-rich fluid respectively, rather than the endocrine hormone pancreatic polypeptide.

questions.stem: Mature insulin is produced by cleaving which connecting component from proinsulin?
questions.why: Processing proinsulin releases insulin and connecting peptide in equimolar amounts.

questions.stem: High insulin with very low C-peptide during hypoglycaemia most strongly suggests what?
questions.why: Injected insulin lacks C-peptide whereas endogenous insulin is released with C-peptide.

questions.stem: After beta-cell glucose metabolism raises ATP, which membrane event begins insulin secretion?
questions.why: Closure of KATP channels depolarizes the cell and opens calcium channels.

questions.stem: Sulfonylureas stimulate beta-cell insulin output principally by what mechanism?

options.label: B
options.text: Blocking glucose entry into beta cells

questions.why: Sulfonylureas close KATP channels via SUR1 to trigger depolarization.

questions.stem: Why does oral glucose produce more insulin than equivalent intravenous glucose?
questions.why: Gut incretins amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release.

questions.stem: Which autonomic receptor stimulation acutely suppresses insulin secretion?
questions.why: Alpha-2 sympathetic signalling suppresses beta-cell insulin secretion.

questions.stem: Insulin disappears rapidly from plasma chiefly through clearance by which organs?
questions.why: Hepatic and renal uptake account for much insulin degradation.

questions.stem: Which tissue increases glucose entry mainly through insulin-induced GLUT4 recruitment?
questions.why: Insulin translocates GLUT4 in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

questions.stem: Which change follows insulin signalling in the liver after a carbohydrate-rich meal?
questions.why: Insulin suppresses glucose production and promotes glycogen synthesis.

questions.stem: Which effect of insulin on protein metabolism is most characteristic?
questions.why: Insulin promotes amino acid uptake and protein anabolism.

questions.stem: Which process explains falling free fatty acids after a meal as insulin rises?
questions.why: Insulin suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase and enhances lipid storage.

questions.stem: Insulin given with glucose for severe hyperkalaemia achieves which immediate shift?
questions.why: Insulin stimulates Na-K ATPase and shifts K into cells; glucose reduces hypoglycaemia risk.

questions.stem: During exercise, contracting skeletal muscles take up glucose even with low insulin. How?
questions.why: Exercise recruits GLUT4 through contraction-dependent pathways.

questions.stem: Insulin deficiency increases hepatic ketone production mainly by supplying which fuel?
questions.why: Enhanced adipose lipolysis supplies fatty acids for hepatic beta-oxidation and ketogenesis.

questions.stem: Why does marked hyperglycaemia cause excessive urine volume?
questions.why: When the reabsorptive threshold is exceeded, tubular glucose retains water.

questions.stem: Deep rapid Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis compensates for what?
questions.why: The respiratory centre drives hyperventilation to reduce CO2 during metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: Which chronic diabetic complication primarily involves small-vessel pathology?
questions.why: Retinopathy is a classic microvascular complication, as are nephropathy and neuropathy.

questions.stem: An obese adult has high circulating insulin but raised glucose. Which initial defect is most likely?
questions.why: Early type 2 diabetes often includes insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia.

questions.stem: Sweating and confusion after excessive insulin occur because the brain is deprived of what?
questions.why: Severe hypoglycaemia causes adrenergic symptoms and neuroglycopenia.

questions.stem: Hyperglycaemia, dehydration and hypotension in uncontrolled diabetes are linked mainly by what?
questions.why: Glucosuria causes osmotic water and electrolyte loss, reducing circulating volume.

questions.stem: During fasting, glucagon raises plasma glucose mainly through which liver pathways?
questions.why: Glucagon increases hepatic glycogen breakdown and new glucose production.

questions.stem: Which metabolic signal usually reduces alpha-cell glucagon secretion?
questions.why: Glucose elevation and local beta-cell signals normally suppress glucagon.

questions.stem: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits anterior pituitary GH secretion directly?
questions.why: Somatostatin inhibits somatotroph secretion, whereas GHRH stimulates it.

questions.stem: Vasopressin increases collecting-duct water permeability chiefly by inserting which channel?
questions.why: V2-receptor signalling promotes apical aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells.

questions.stem: Deficiency of GH before epiphyseal fusion can primarily cause which growth disturbance?
questions.why: Low GH or IGF-1 during childhood reduces linear skeletal growth.

questions.stem: A hormone is released through a neural rather than hypophyseal portal pathway. Which example is correct?
questions.why: Posterior pituitary hormones are released from hypothalamic axon terminals.

questions.stem: Longstanding severe dietary iodine deficiency can enlarge the thyroid mainly through which response?
questions.why: Low thyroid hormone reduces negative feedback and raises TSH-driven follicular growth.

questions.stem: Which protein scaffold is secreted by follicular cells into colloid for hormone synthesis?
questions.why: Thyroglobulin provides tyrosyl residues for iodination and coupling.

questions.stem: The major intracellular second messenger used by the TSH receptor is which?
questions.why: TSH receptor signalling is mainly Gs-coupled and activates cyclic AMP pathways.

questions.stem: Why does T4 persist longer in plasma than the more potent T3?
questions.why: T4 is more extensively bound and generally has a longer circulating half-life.

questions.stem: Thyroid hormone promotes carbohydrate availability partly through which gastrointestinal effect?
questions.why: Thyroid hormone increases intestinal carbohydrate absorption and supports gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem: Which normal total plasma calcium range is given in the lecture slides?
questions.why: The calcium metabolism slides list total plasma calcium at approximately 2.16–2.65 mmol/L.

questions.stem: High alkaline phosphatase activity in bone is especially associated with which cells?
questions.why: Osteoblasts express bone alkaline phosphatase during osteoid mineralization.

questions.stem: What is the main role of ultraviolet light in endogenous vitamin D metabolism?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatic conversion of calcidiol to calcitriol

options.label: B
options.text: Renal conversion of calcitriol to calcidiol

options.label: C
options.text: Gut conversion of vitamin D to calcitonin

options.label: E
options.text: Bone conversion of calcium to phosphate

questions.why: UVB drives the skin reaction that forms previtamin D3 from 7-dehydrocholesterol.

questions.stem: Which vitamin D metabolite is formed mainly by hepatic 25-hydroxylation?
questions.why: The liver generates 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the major circulating storage marker.

questions.stem: Why does excess cortisol increase susceptibility to infection even when leukocyte counts appear elevated?
questions.why: Glucocorticoids suppress immune activation and inflammatory mediator production.

questions.stem: Why can primary adrenal failure cause metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia?
questions.why: Aldosterone deficiency reduces distal potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.

questions.stem: Which acute condition stimulates adrenal catecholamine secretion as part of stress physiology?
questions.why: Hypoglycaemia activates the sympathetic-adrenal medullary response.

questions.stem: Why may thiazide-associated hypokalaemia impair pancreatic insulin secretion?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased plasma potassium opens KATP channels

questions.why: Potassium depletion can impair beta-cell excitability and insulin release, contributing to thiazide-associated hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: Type 1 diabetes usually begins with which predominant physiological deficit?
questions.why: Type 1 diabetes involves severe beta-cell loss and absolute insulin deficiency.

questions.stem: Pancreatic glucagon is secreted predominantly from which islet cell?
questions.why: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, while beta cells release insulin.
